Chasles

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Move six dots around an oval and see where lines through them cross.
How to play: Drag A to F along the oval, or drag a small corner dot to change the oval's shape. Focus a dot and use the arrow keys instead, and press Show names to label the crossings.
Look for the math

Six points on one oval make a hexagon. Draw lines through pairs of them and the crossings look as if they could wander anywhere — but one pair always lands on the very same spot. The proof on the applet's page was suggested by Hubert Shutrick.

Four lines from one point

Pick four points on a conic and draw the four lines to them from a fifth point of the conic. Those four lines form a pencil. Their cross-ratio is a single number made from the four lines; for four points on any straight line cutting the pencil it is ((c-a)/(c-b)) / ((d-a)/(d-b)), using signed positions along that line.

Chasles' theorem

Move the fifth point somewhere else on the conic: the cross-ratio does not change. That is Chasles' theorem. In the picture, P is AB ^ DE, Q is CD ^ FA, and the blue line p joins them. It cuts the conic at L and M and meets AD at T.

Where the crossings meet

Now put R = EF ^ p and S = BC ^ p. Cutting the pencils from F and D by the blue line gives (LQRM) = F(LAEM) = D(LAEM) = (LTPM). Cutting the pencils from A and C gives (LTPM) = A(LDBM) = C(LDBM) = (LQSM). Chasles' theorem is used once in each chain, so (LQRM) = (LQSM). Three points of a line and their cross-ratio pin down the fourth, hence R = S — the three Pascal crossings are collinear, which is Pascal's theorem.

Checked, not just claimed

The logic test drags the ellipse and all six points into hundreds of shapes. In every usable one it measures both cross-ratios independently, from the signed angles at the two vertices and from positions along the blue line, and confirms the whole chain above and R = S. It also compares every constructed point with a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode computation.

Try moving every point to one side of the ellipse, so the hexagon is very lopsided. The blue line swings, but R and S still sit on top of each other.
